articles.title: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
articles.summary: Recent polls suggest the president is facing challenging headwinds in the state ahead of the midterms.
articles.body:
It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel.

The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself.

As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest.

"I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname.

In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys.

During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers.

Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

"They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing.

"But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight."

After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said.

"The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added.

Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy.

This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year.

Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered.

Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate.

Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem.

"I remember I put out a video… thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all."

But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added.

Recent polls suggest much of Trump's support among Hispanic voters has ebbed away since 2024. Surveys taken since late summer indicate a majority of Texan Hispanic voters disapprove of the president. They also suggest Hispanic voters are favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.

"When I voted for President Trump, I voted for him because we saw an influx of immigration during the Biden administration," said Mario Guerrero, a young Mexican-American businessman who leads the South Texas Builders Association. It needed to be fixed, he said.

"We thought that we were in the right by voting for Trump, and that he was going to do what was best in order to fix the crisis on the border.

"And I think to myself, we were really not told the extreme that they were willing to go to make a point," he added, before referencing recent shootings involving ICE agents in US cities.

Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues.

A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration.

Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown.

"There's a man that I know that… last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work."

Even though Guerrero plans to vote Democrat, he describes himself as neither Democrat nor Republican. And that, according to Mike Madrid, a leading Republican consultant and expert on Hispanic voters, is key to understanding the largest ethnic demographic voting group in the country.

"Latinos are more likely than any other racial or ethnic group to identify as independents rather than Republicans or Democrats," he said.

It was in part the belief that Hispanic voters were shifting permanently towards the Republican Party that led Trump to press states such as Texas to redraw their congressional maps early, before the once-a-decade census.

The strategy was intended to capitalise on what Republicans saw as a realignment in Hispanic voting behaviour, particularly in border districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century.

Texas's 15th congressional district was among those that were redrawn, and has become one of the clearest tests of whether electoral maps can guarantee political outcomes.

The seat was redrawn after the 2020 census and was won by a Republican in 2022. It was redrawn again in 2025, creating a notional 18-point majority for Republicans in these midterms. Even so, current polling suggests a Democratic lead of five or six points.

Bobby Pulido is the Democratic candidate hoping to win the district. As a popular Tejano singer and winner of two Latin Grammys, he is already a household name in the Rio Grande Valley.

At an event just weeks before the vote, he delivered a stock political speech followed by a musical performance. "A lot of people are disillusioned with both parties," he told the BBC shortly before he took the stage. "And I hear them."

To win in this part of Texas, you need to be a conservative. Pulido has distanced himself from the national Democratic Party brand and focused deliberately and consistently on economic issues.

"This isn't New York, this isn't LA," he said. "When you lead with issues like social justice, climate change and other topics, that's not what people want to hear first. They want to hear about the economy."

That message is consistent with what many current polls are suggesting - the economy, and the cost of living specifically, rank top on the list of most voters' priorities.

At a local avocado festival, a fruit that is a staple among Hispanic communities in the valley, a couple, Dave Baldwin and Veronica Salazar, began discussing rising prices as soon as they were asked about the upcoming elections.

When asked who they blame for spiking costs, the answer was swift. "The president," they said.

"He is in control of our destiny with all that, and right now he's not doing a very good job," added Baldwin.

Among many Republican campaigners here, there is a feeling that they are are on the back foot just weeks before the vote.

Alexis Uscanga, a student volunteer tasked with knocking on doors and checking on likely Republican voters in the district, was realistic about what he is trying to achieve.

"The midterms are just purely a game of turnout," he said. "It's not trying so much to convince individuals to vote one way or the other, it's about trying to get our people mostly to show up."

Tano Tijerina, the Republican candidate in the neighbouring, Democratic-held 28th district, credited Trump with "breaking through barriers" but acknowledged the "national political headwinds are real".

The Hispanic shift towards President Trump in 2024 was one of the most striking political facts of the past decade. While this expanding demographic may not have much love for either party, in a two-party system voters are mostly forced to make a choice.

And if polling is correct - and there is no guarantee of that - even a modest swing back to Democrats in November could reshape races not just across this state but far beyond.

In Texas, it could even be enough to put a US Senate seat in play - and Democrats haven't won one of those in the state in more than 30 years.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

articles.title: An Indiana homeowner chopped down shrubs, trampled tulips and tore up landscaping lights in a shared garden, calling it routine maintenance; after an HOA went to court, an appeals panel upheld the injunction
articles.summary: An Indiana homeowner who cut down shrubs, trampled flowers and damaged landscaping lights in a shared garden has lost his appeal against an order
articles.body: An Indiana homeowner who cut down shrubs, trampled flowers and damaged landscaping lights in a shared garden has lost his appeal against an order preventing further damage to common areas. In its decision published by Justia, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld a preliminary injunction obtained by the Efroymson House Owner’s Association against Martin L. Booth. Booth described his actions as routine maintenance, but the court found sufficient evidence that the association controlled the shared landscaping and had a reasonable likelihood of succeeding in its vandalism claim. The ruling allows the injunction to remain in place while the underlying dispute continues.How the garden dispute beganThe case concerned a property in Indianapolis that included an early twentieth-century house and a carriage house. Between 2016 and 2018, the owner added a garage with a dwelling above it. Booth entered into an agreement to purchase the property in 2018 and received a warranty deed in February 2020. Before the purchase was completed, the original lot had been divided into three parcels. In May 2019, the owner recorded a declaration establishing covenants, conditions, easements and restrictions, known as CCRs, and providing for the creation of the homeowners’ association.The declaration designated certain areas, including part of Booth’s parcel, as common areas. It gave the HOA responsibility for maintaining and repairing these spaces, as well as authority to install improvements and manage, maintain and replace them. Around 2023, the association installed landscaping that included arborvitae shrubs, tulips, other plants, lighting and a bench. The dispute arose over Booth’s actions in these shared areas and whether he could alter the landscaping without the association’s permission.Shrubs, flowers and lights were damagedAccording to the court’s account, Booth entered the common areas without the HOA’s consent on April 14, 2026, and cut shrubs and other plants. He also trampled tulips and other flowers and damaged additional vegetation. The following day, he returned and chopped down an eight-foot-tall arborvitae shrub with an axe. He pulled another shrub out of the ground, tipped over a bench and tore landscaping lights from the ground.The HOA’s president, Kevin Krulewitch, witnessed the actions on both days and asked Booth to stop. According to the court record, Booth refused and maintained that he could do what he wanted with what he considered his property. Booth acknowledged his actions during the proceedings but characterised them as routine maintenance. He also argued that his contractual interest in the property predated the recorded restrictions. The association disputed his position, maintaining that Booth had purchased the property subject to the restrictions and that the HOA had authority over the common areas.Why the HOA sought an injunctionOn April 16, 2026, the association sued Booth, alleging vandalism and seeking civil damages under Indiana’s Crime Victims Relief Act. It also requested an emergency restraining order and a preliminary injunction to prevent further damage. The trial court issued an emergency restraining order the next day. Following a hearing, it granted the preliminary injunction on May 6, finding that the HOA had demonstrated a reasonable likelihood of success in its claim, that it faced irreparable harm without the order and that the balance of harms favoured the association.The court required the HOA to post a $100 surety bond, which provides security for potential costs or damages if an injunction is later found to have been wrongfully issued. Booth challenged the injunction, disputing the bond amount, the exclusion of evidence and the findings supporting the order. He argued that monetary damages could address any harm instead of restricting his actions.The appeals court rejected his arguments, explaining that an injunction can be appropriate when preventing continuing damage is more practical than repeatedly seeking compensation after the event. The judges also considered evidence that Booth intended to continue his activities in the common areas.Appeals court upholds the injunctionThe Indiana Court of Appeals concluded that the HOA had presented sufficient evidence that Booth intentionally damaged landscaping in areas the association was entitled to manage and control. The absence of the HOA’s consent supported its claim under state vandalism law. The panel also found no abuse of discretion in setting the bond at $100. It concluded that Booth had not adequately demonstrated that the trial court wrongly excluded his proposed evidence.The judges affirmed the preliminary injunction, leaving the restrictions on Booth’s actions in place while the underlying case proceeds. The ruling did not finally determine liability or damages. The Court of Appeals issued the ruling as a memorandum decision, which is not binding precedent under Indiana law. The decision highlights how homeowners’ associations can seek court protection when property owners allegedly damage shared spaces.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: As global corporations and government agencies scrambled to patch critical, newly uncovered vulnerabilities in PHP – the foundational programming language that powers a majority of the worldwide web – top technology executives, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, reacted to the unfolding crisis during an industry event in Germany this week. This comment came as security firms recorded millions of automated exploitation attempts within hours of the bug’s public disclosure.“I’ve not seen anything like this in a long, long time. It was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks,” Nadella said, stressing that the incident highlights how vital it is to build maintainable, secure software as architectures grow exponentially complex, as per news agency Reuters.Government and public websites go darkFrom Tokyo to Helsinki, emergency shutdowns hit banking portals, rail services, flight bookings, tax departments and municipal communications – triggering one of the most severe real-world stress tests ever faced by the aging, open-source codebases that keep people online.PHP operates as an essential web-building block alongside fundamental standards like HTML and Python. On Wednesday (October 21), the core development team behind PHP published emergency security patches for flaws that had sat undetected within the code for years before being brought to light using artificial intelligence. The team urged users across the globe to “update immediately.”However, the timing of the release created severe exposure. Madeline Lawrence, co-founder of Belgian cybersecurity firm Aikido Security, noted that technical details surrounding the bugs entered the public domain before organizations were ready with deployed patches, triggering immediate exploitation.“Companies are racing to update against attackers who can use AI to exploit them. That’s the whole race,” Lawrence said. The scale of the threat was confirmed by network performance and security provider Cloudflare, which tracked an immediate, exponential surge in automated intrusions hitting its global infrastructure.Posting on X (formerly Twitter), Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince broke down the staggering timeline:10 Hours Prior to Public Disclosure: Thousands of probing attempts were logged across the network.45 Minutes Post-Announcement: Attack volumes jumped to tens of thousands.2 Hours Post-Announcement: Exploitation attempts escalated into hundreds of thousands.Current Volume: Sustained attack runs have surged into the millions.Fearing catastrophic data compromises, dozens of major corporations and state ministries chose to sever public access entirely while engineers raced to deploy patches. articles.title: A Winston Churchill painting made in 1948 sold at Christie's for £716,800 in London; the auction house says all of the hammer-price proceeds will support the Churchill Fellowship, turning artwork into charity funding
articles.summary: A painting of flowers by former British prime minister Winston Churchill has sold for £716,800 at Christie’s in London, with all of the hammer-price
articles.body: A painting of flowers by former British prime minister Winston Churchill has sold for £716,800 at Christie’s in London, with all of the hammer-price proceeds set to support a charity programme promoting arts in public spaces. The painting, Amaryllis Lily, was sold during Christie’s Modern British and Irish Art Evening Sale on October 21, 2026. According to the auction house’s official results, 100% of the hammer price will benefit the Churchill Fellowship, turning a work from Churchill’s personal art collection into funding for community-focused arts initiatives.The painting, created in 1948, had been estimated to sell for between £300,000 and £500,000 before the auction. Its final price exceeded the upper end of that estimate by £216,800. Christie’s confirmed the sale in its results announcement and said the money would help fund the Fellowship’s “Making Space for the Arts” programme.The £716,800 figure represents the price realised at auction, but the charity’s share is specifically defined as the hammer price. It should not be confused with the buyer’s total bill, which can include the auction house’s buyer’s premium and other applicable charges.A painting passed from father to daughterAmaryllis Lily is an oil painting on canvas measuring 36 by 24 inches, or approximately 91.5 by 61 centimetres. Christie’s catalogue records Churchill’s initials, “WSC”, in the lower-left corner. The work’s ownership history gives it a personal connection to the Churchill family. According to the auction catalogue, Churchill gifted the painting to his youngest daughter, Lady Mary Soames. She subsequently donated it in 1995 to the Winston Churchill Memorial Trust, now known as the Churchill Fellowship, allowing the organisation to use the artwork at its discretion to support its work.The painting was therefore held by the charity for more than three decades before being offered at auction. Its sale allows the organisation to convert an artwork associated with Churchill’s private life into financial support for its programmes.Churchill is best known internationally for leading Britain during the Second World War and serving as prime minister, but painting was also an important personal pursuit. He began painting in 1915 and continued for decades, producing landscapes, still lifes and scenes inspired by his travels.Christie’s noted that the artist Walter Richard Sickert had a practical influence on Churchill’s painting, introducing him to the technique of working from photographs. Amaryllis Lily reflects Churchill’s interest in still-life subjects, which allowed him to explore colour, composition and the arrangement of objects.Where the auction money will goThe proceeds are intended to support the Churchill Fellowship’s “Making Space for the Arts” programme, a three-year initiative launched in 2025. The programme seeks to strengthen artistic practice in public spaces and broaden access to cultural activities.According to the Fellowship’s official website, the initiative supports projects that explore how large-scale artistic activity can be designed and delivered with communities. It also aims to expand participation in public arts, making cultural experiences more inclusive and relevant to people in different places.Public arts projects can take place in settings such as streets, parks, public buildings, coastlines and rural landscapes, rather than being restricted to traditional galleries and theatres. Such activities can give communities opportunities to participate in creative work, express local identities and experience art collectively.The Fellowship says the programme is intended to develop the skills, knowledge and approaches needed to deliver ambitious public arts projects. It is seeking a second cohort of around 10 Fellows to build on the programme’s initial work.The organisation also points to pressures facing the arts sector, including reduced local government cultural funding in parts of the UK and the closure of some traditional venues. Its programme aims to help practitioners develop new approaches to public-facing artistic activity.The auction proceeds will contribute to this work, although Christie’s has not said that the sale alone will finance the entire programme.Churchill’s legacy supports a modern causeThe Churchill Fellowship, the operating name of the Winston Churchill Memorial Trust, is a UK charity established in 1965. It awards fellowships that enable people to learn from approaches and practices in other countries and apply those lessons in the UK.The sale of Amaryllis Lily illustrates one way the charity can use a historical asset to support contemporary projects. Rather than remaining solely a collectible associated with a prominent historical figure, the painting has generated funds for a programme focused on participation, creativity and public spaces.The auction took place as part of Christie’s October sale of modern British and Irish art. The evening auction raised £23.09 million in total, according to the auction house. The highest-selling work was Barbara Hepworth’s sculpture Sculpture with Colour (Eos), which achieved £6.19 million.Churchill’s painting was among the works whose sale carried a specific charitable purpose. Its £716,800 result exceeded its pre-sale estimate, while the commitment to direct the hammer-price proceeds to the Fellowship ensures that the transaction also supports the charity’s ongoing work.For the organisation, the sale represents more than the disposal of a painting. It provides a source of funding for an initiative intended to bring artistic activity into shared spaces and encourage more people to participate in cultural life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran under mounting oil pressure: Will Tehran hit back over US blockade?
articles.summary: The US naval blockade on Iranian ports has weakened Tehran’s ability to generate revenue from oil exports, potentially pushing Iran to intensify efforts
articles.body: The US naval blockade on Iranian ports has weakened Tehran’s ability to generate revenue from oil exports, potentially pushing Iran to intensify efforts to break the blockade and challenge Washington’s restrictions.Iran is facing mounting financial pressure as the blockade curbs oil revenue, while cryptocurrency offers only a limited alternative for moving money, former US Treasury official Miad Maleki said in an interview with Iran International.The freezing of around $350 million in Iranian cryptocurrency and Washington’s claim that the blockade has prevented at least $25 billion in Iranian oil exports highlight the growing strain on Tehran’s finances. Maleki said, however, that the loss of oil revenue posed the greater challenge for Iran.Blockade cuts off billions in oil revenueUS Central Command commander Admiral Brad Cooper said on Thursday that the maritime blockade had prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil over 100 days.Iran initially continued selling oil that had passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the blockade and remained aboard tankers in international waters. However, those floating reserves were depleted by mid-October, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing analysts at commodity-data firm Kpler.“There’s no more oil to discharge to China anymore,” Kpler’s head of crude oil analysis Homayoun Falakshahi told the Journal.“The economic clock of the Islamic Republic has basically stopped,” Maleki said, arguing that Tehran no longer had access to the oil revenue it previously relied on to finance imports.Import costs pose next challenge for TehranSome goods currently entering Iran were paid for earlier, while other imports continue to arrive through land routes, Maleki said.He warned that financial pressure would intensify when Tehran has to pay for new purchases and transportation costs without the oil revenue it previously relied on.“When they can no longer pay the cost of buying and transporting the goods they are now importing over land, that is when the problems will become much more difficult for the Islamic Republic,” Maleki said.He cautioned, however, that it remained difficult to determine how quickly Iran would reach that point.Yemen government forces consolidate control as Houthis target Saudi infrastructureMeanwhile, Yemeni government-aligned forces are continuing to consolidate control over territory along the southern end of the Red Sea coastal plain.The Houthis are continuing to attack Saudi government, civilian and oil infrastructure in an effort to pressure Riyadh into withdrawing its support for the Yemeni government and accepting Houthi demands.You use AI every day. articles.body: The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to prevent voters from using student identity cards as a backup form of voter ID in the upcoming midterm elections, siding with the state in an emergency appeal backed by Republicans.The order was issued on Thursday, less than two weeks before voters head to the polls in a closely contested US Senate race. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the court to dissent publicly.The dispute centres on a New Hampshire law passed this year that removed student IDs from the list of identification documents expressly accepted for voting. The state's secretary of state subsequently issued guidance barring students from using those cards as an alternative means of establishing their identity at polling stations.A judge allowed the law to remain in effect but blocked the secretary of state's guidance in early October. The state then appealed to the Supreme Court, receiving support from the Republican National Committee.In granting the emergency appeal, the justices relied on the legal principle that courts should generally avoid changing election rules shortly before voting takes place.State Representative Donald McFarlane, who sponsored the bill, argued that colleges do not apply the same safeguards as government agencies when issuing student identification cards.“Today’s Supreme Court decision is a victory for common sense,” McFarlane said in an email. “It allows HB 323 to work as intended: strengthening voter identity verification, applying a consistent standard, and maintaining public confidence in New Hampshire elections.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Bridgend man in court charged with murder of Eleanor Barnfield
articles.summary: Clifford Foster, 61, from Bridgend, appeared at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday morning.
articles.body:
A 61-year-old man has appeared in court charged with the murder of a woman who suffered "stab wounds" and died following a crash.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to a crash on Coity Road in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision". The BBC understands they were sustained in a stabbing.

Clifford Foster was arrested on Tuesday at the Ger-y-Nant retirement housing complex, close to where the crash happened, where he lived and Eleanor worked.

Speaking only to confirm his name, age and address, Foster appeared at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday, wearing a grey tracksuit and using a crutch to support himself.

The incident led to a significant police operation, with specially trained firearm officers involved in a "stand off" at the retirement complex which lasted 12 hours, before an arrest at 01:00 BST on Tuesday.

Reports in some media had claimed Eleanor had crashed her car while driving herself to hospital.

On Thursday, the Welsh Ambulance Service (WAS) denied Eleanor was driving because of ambulance wait times , saying it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online.

It said medics were called to the crash on Coity Road at about 12:44 and a response unit arrived seven minutes later, adding two emergency ambulances then arrived to provide additional support at 13:07 and 13:13.

It described the rumours on social media as "contradictory" and "factually untrue".

"We would encourage members of the public not to speculate," the service said.

In a statement on Thursday, WAS said initial investigations were "unable to identify" any calls from Eleanor's phone numbers.

It said enquiries were ongoing to "establish if any calls were received by other means".

In a tribute, Eleanor was described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world".

"She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock," they added.

The police confirmed the murder was not being investigated as a domestic incident, and encouraged the public "to not speculate about the circumstances" as court proceedings were now active.

Foster remains remanded in custody and will appear at Cardiff Crown Court on 26 October.

articles.title: Meet Archana Jaisal: Her father went from pulling a rickshaw to getting a railway job through education; now she brings Rs 100 coaching to rural children
articles.summary: Archana Jaisal grew up witnessing how education could transform destiny.
articles.body: Archana Jaisal grew up witnessing how education could transform destiny. When she saw kids in rural Uttar Pradesh struggling with basic lessons despite going to school, she was reminded of her own journey. She very well knew how education could change lives so, through Shiksha Saathi, she is bringing affordable learning opportunities to rural children while helping local women become financially independent.Meet Archana JaisalHer father, Jagdish Ram, had experienced the same struggle. As a teenager, he used to pull a rickshaw to support his family while also managing studies. Eventually, education helped him secure a railway job and provide for his children.Years later, Archana decided to carry that legacy forward through Shiksha Saathi, a rural education initiative offering affordable after-school coaching and training local women as teachers.According to The Better India report, the organisation operates more than 78 learning centres across six districts of Uttar Pradesh, reaching over 7,650 students with 67 teachers. Its monthly coaching fees start at Rs 100 for younger children, while those unable to afford the fees are also accommodated.From pulling a rickshaw to getting a railway jobFor Archana, her father is her hero, her inspiration. After losing his father at a young age, Jagdish began pulling a rickshaw at 17 to support his family. Despite the financial pressure, he continued studying and eventually graduated. His circumstances began to change when a fellow rickshaw puller suggested that he apply for a railway job after noticing him studying regularly.Jagdish applied and got the job. He moved to Varanasi. While waiting for his career to settle, he took up additional work, painting banners, making portraits and writing names and numbers on T-shirts.However, the family faced another setback when he died while Archana was still young. With their mother unable to take up his railway job, the siblings struggled financially. Archana’s elder sister began earning to support the household and pay for tuition.Archana eventually completed her graduation and post-graduation in Economics from Banaras Hindu University.Beginning of her initiativeArchana saw that some children in her extended family struggled with basic questions, even in Class 7. She realised that many needed additional academic support but could not afford expensive private coaching. At the same time, educated girls and women in villages had limited employment opportunities.In 2022, Archana launched Your Coaching, which was formally registered as Shiksha Saathi in 2023. The initiative brings after-school learning closer to children, offering coaching for students from Classes 1 to 12.Monthly fees range from Rs 100 for younger students to Rs 600 for those in Class 12, according to The Better India. Children from financially disadvantaged families can attend without paying.Its training programme prepares rural girls and women to teach children according to their learning levels. More than 740 women have reportedly completed the programme, creating opportunities for them to earn while supporting education in their own communities.How teaching is changing women’s livesNeetu, who became a Shiksha Saathi teacher at 19, is one example of this approach. Initially nervous about teaching, she received training and classroom support that helped her gain confidence.She now earns around Rs 6,000 to Rs 7,000 a month, as per reports. “I started paying for my own studies and coaching, so I no longer needed to take money from home,” she said.From fearing Maths to dreaming of becoming a teacherRiya, a 10-year-old who has attended the institute for three years, once feared Maths. With teachers explaining concepts and answering her questions, the subject became her favourite.“When I used to study Maths before, I used to feel scared. Now, things have changed,” she said. She now hopes to become a teacher herself.Today, the institute operates across Bhadohi, Varanasi, Mirzapur, Prayagraj, Mau and Ghazipur. Its activities also include youth competitions that encourage children to think about their ambitions and future careers.For Archana, every child who begins to believe in their abilities represents a continuation of the opportunity her father fought so hard to secure for his own family.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cypriot police open investigation into Roman Abramovich's assets
articles.summary: Questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers, were raised earlier this month.
articles.body:
Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.

Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).

A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.

Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".

The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.

The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.

Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.

The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.

The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation.

A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.

When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."

He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."

Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.

Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.

The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.

Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT.

Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

articles.title: South Korea invites North for military talks over border
articles.summary: The proposal comes days after Pyongyang says it moved new military units into ‘firing positions’ along the border.
articles.body:
South Korea has proposed holding military talks with North Korea in a bid to calm rising tensions over their heavily fortified border.

Seoul said on Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.

Talks with North Korea would aim to “mutually confirm” the precise location of the land Military Demarcation Line (MDL), “discuss ways to restore military communication lines and prevent accidental clashes in border areas”, Kim Hong-cheol, deputy minister for national defence policy, told reporters.

“Specific dates and locations could be discussed through Panmunjom,” Kim said, referring to the symbolic truce village on the North-South border where soldiers from both Koreas stand face to face.

He added that the South was open to three-way talks involving the United States-led United Nations Command and hoped for “a positive response from North Korea”.

It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim Jong Un has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.

Meanwhile, Pyongyang has raised its military activity along the border and continues to do so.

On Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, announced that new military units have been moved into “firing positions” along the border.

Mines, barbed-wire fences, tactical roads, antitank walls and other fortifications have also been added to one of the world’s most heavily armed borders.

Tensions have worsened since last month when three South Korean soldiers were injured by explosions near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone, the buffer zone that runs between the Koreas, commonly known as the DMZ.

The South blamed the blast on landmines laid by the North and demanded an apology . Pyongyang has fiercely rejected the accusation.

Seoul’s Ministry of National Defence said on Friday that it was difficult to predict “what further incidents could occur if this situation is allowed to continue unaddressed”.

The ministry noted that a proposal for talks last year did not receive a response from Pyongyang.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has called for the North to return to dialogue. However, Kim Yo Jong responded by slamming the suggestion of bilateral talks as “the climax of the farce”.

articles.title: 'Time has come': Commonwealth chief urges King Charles to apologise for Britain's role in slave trade, calls for reparations talks
articles.summary: Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey calls on King Charles III to apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade and initiate discussions on reparations, as the upcoming Caribbean tour looms. This article discusses the demands from Commonwealth nations, the implications of the King's visit, and the ongoing debate on reparations.
articles.body: Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey has called on King Charles III to apologise for Britain's historical role in the slave trade, saying the “time has come” for countries to discuss reparations for the harm caused by slavery.In an interview with Sky News, Botchwey said several Commonwealth countries wanted an apology from the monarch ahead of his upcoming Caribbean tour. Asked whether he should apologise, she said: “That’s what the countries have asked for... It wouldn’t hurt to have that. Not at all.”“I don't believe we can run away from it,” she added. “But it is important to determine the form that reparations should take, and that is something that will emerge eventually.”Botchwey said countries should decide collectively how reparations could work, including whether they should involve financial compensation or other forms of support.“Us as countries sit around the table to discuss, as difficult a subject as it is, I believe that countries will come to some conclusions,” she said.She said possible measures could include “concessional financing”, the return of artefacts and action on climate-related issues.The debate is expected to feature during the King's eight-day visit to three Caribbean nations, as well as at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where reparations are likely to be a contentious issue.However, the King is not expected to issue a formal apology or offer reparations, in line with government advice. Buckingham Palace has said he will use the visit to acknowledge the historical wrongs associated with slavery.A Palace spokesperson said: “It is important to note here the work His Majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to ‘right inequalities that endure’.”The spokesperson added that the visit would provide opportunities to “reflect and renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment” to that process.The Palace has previously said the King takes the issue of slavery and reparations “very seriously” and “feels personal sorrow at the suffering of so many”.Botchwey, Ghana's former foreign minister, became Commonwealth secretary-general after Baroness Patricia Scotland stepped down in March last year. She has previously expressed support for financial reparations and said the issue should be discussed by member states.Jamaica takes reparations petition to the KingThe renewed calls come as Caribbean campaigners seek compensation for the slave trade and its lasting effects. Envoys from Jamaica and other former British colonies have urged the King to support their campaign.Last month, Jamaica's culture minister, Olivia Grange, led a delegation to London to submit a petition to the monarch. Grange later told Jamaica's parliament that the King had referred the matter to the Privy Council, which remains the country's highest court of appeal under legislation dating back to the 19th century.Grange described the referral as a “big deal”, saying the King could have ignored the petition or declined to refer the questions for consideration.A hearing has provisionally been scheduled for the week of March 8, 2027. The committee could consider whether slavery was illegal and whether Britain has a legal obligation to provide a remedy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Of the many roles Chris Pratt plays in his life, the one he says matters most is the one he is least likely to win an award for: father.
articles.body: Of the many roles Chris Pratt plays in his life, the one he says matters most is the one he is least likely to win an award for: father. The Terminal List actor is married to author Katherine Schwarzenegger, and they have three children together. Pratt also has a son, Jack, with his ex-wife, actress Anna Faris. In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Chris Pratt spoke about how his faith shapes his parenting. He starts each day with it, and faith is the ‘most important’ thing he wants his children to inherit, above everything else he can give them.“My faith is how I start my day; it's how I end my day,” Chris Pratt told the outlet.Faith is the most important thing for Chris PrattChris Pratt has talked about God in public for years. Ahead of the season 2 release of The Terminal List, the actor opened up about raising four kids in Hollywood while keeping his Christian faith at the centre of their lives. Faith is how he starts and ends each day, and he wants it to be a part of his children's lives as well.“Oh, God, you know, I'm, for the most part, always gonna be a man of faith. My faith is how I start my day; it's how I end my day. It's the most important thing that I'll be able to pass on to my kids,” the actor told the outlet.Chris Pratt has always been vocal about his beliefs. At the 2018 Teen Choice Awards, he said, “I want to thank God.” He also told the young audience that they should love God as he does.“I always do that when I’m up on a big platform in front of a bunch of young faces. I say, ‘I love God!’ That’s my thing, I love Him and you should too!” He also weighed in on how the world assumes Hollywood is anti-religious. “I think that there’s this narrative that exists out there that Hollywood is anti-Christian or anti-religious, but it’s just not the case,” he said. “They are kind of not anti-anything. They are kind of pro whatever is authentic to you. And I like that. Because it’s authentic for me to be pro-Christian, pro-Jesus. That’s my thing. I like it.”Pratt’s openness has drawn criticism. Despite the criticism, the actor has continued to speak openly about his faith and his belief that God has a plan for his life.Fatherhood and faithChris Pratt is a father of four. For him, it is the best role he has had in his life. Though the role demands a lot, he wouldn’t trade it for anything else. “It's an incredible blessing to be a father. It's also a lot of hard work. And so I think I just want to teach them that... I don't know, I want to do my best. I basically want to get right everything my dad got right and get right everything my dad got wrong. And I'm sure I'll screw up both, you know?” Pratt said.It was during his son Jack’s infancy that Pratt’s religious beliefs grew stronger. In 2012, his son with his then-wife, Anna Faris, was born seven weeks premature, weighing only 3 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.“He had all of these issues going on. I prayed hard to God. I was in a season of transition spiritually at that time, and didn't quite fully understand. I made a deal with God again: ‘I'm sorry, God, here I am again, asking for your grace again.’ And He really saved my son, and that was the moment [my faith] was cemented. My heart softened, and my faith hardened,” the actor told the Christian Post previously.He also spoke about how he is ‘unashamed’ of his faith. “I'm a father of four. I want to raise my children with an understanding that their dad was unashamed of his faith in Jesus, and with a profound understanding of the power of prayer, and the grace and the love and the joy that can come from a relationship with Jesus… You don't hear that a lot from people in entertainment, but it's who I am. I'm not going to hide behind it. A city on a hill cannot be hidden,” he told the outlet.Meanwhile, on the professional front, the new season of The Terminal List began premiering on Prime Video on 21 October 2026.You use AI every day. articles.title: Part of Brighton's iconic West Pier collapses
articles.summary: One man tells the BBC he saw a "huge crash" as a big wave hit the side of the East Sussex landmark.
articles.body:
Part of Brighton's West Pier has fallen into the sea during the wet and windy weather.

In footage obtained by the BBC, one side of the famous landmark can be seen collapsing into the water as it is battered by large waves.

Simon Haffenden, who recorded the video, said he saw a "big wave come along and literally hit the pier".

"You heard the bang of the wave and then... there was a huge crash," he told the BBC.

"It was an incredible sound, but it was really shocking.

But Haffenden, a resident of the East Sussex city for 16 years, added he also felt sad seeing part of the pier destroyed.

"It's so iconic," he said. "It's such a beauty".

"It sounds funny to say, but it is such a unique thing to have on the seafront that most other cities don't.

It comes as Storm Austen has brought widespread disruption to Southeast England, with gusts of up to 70mph expected in the region.

The pier was first opened in 1866, with its final building - a concert hall - completed in 1916.

It attracted two million visitors at its peak, though its popularity declined after the Second World War.

The pier closed to the public in 1975 and grew increasingly derelict, but the ruined structure became a symbol of Brighton for some.

Major sections fell into the sea during storms in late 2002, while two separate fires the following year destroyed most of what remained.

English Heritage later declared it beyond repair.

Subsequent storms have destroyed its iron frame even further.

articles.title: Earnings limit of up to £140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
articles.summary: The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed loans for those buying new-builds in England.
articles.body:
Households will need to earn less than £110,000 to qualify for the government's new loan scheme for first-time buyers, or £140,000 for homes bought in London.

As first reported by The Times , the earnings limits are expected to be confirmed at the Budget next week.

The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed equity loans worth 20% of new-build properties in England bought from participating developers.

The loans, which will also be subject to an initial interest-free period, are designed to help people buy a home with deposits as low as 2.5%.

Previous schemes to help first-time buyers did not restrict eligibility by income but faced criticism for stoking house prices by allowing relatively wealthy households to borrow more.

Unveiling the Your First Home Scheme at last month's Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it would focus on those who "really need support".

Details of the changes, including salary caps, are due to be confirmed at next week's Budget.

The Times reported that ministers had initially decided to set the earnings limits at £90,000 for homes outside outside London and £110,000 in the capital, before concluding this would deny access to too many middle-earning couples, such as teachers and nurses.

The government has also argued that the scheme will help to boost housebuilding, after ministers conceded they are set to miss a target to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election.

Labour has said the scheme will be funded by within existing government budgets, but is yet to provide details of which other areas will see their spending cut.

Developers taking part in the scheme will also be asked to contribute towards running costs.

The Home Builders Federation, which represents developers, has welcomed the plans and urged the government to move quickly to set up the scheme.

The Conservatives have however branded the proposals a "colossal admission of failure" of Labour's housebuilding record, and expressed concerns that the new developer levy could push up the price of new homes.

Like the Help to Buy scheme launched under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, the scheme will use equity loans, which are linked to changes in the value of properties they are used to purchase.

That scheme, which initially ran between 2013 and 2021, enabled all home purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home worth up to £600,000.

Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.

A second version of that scheme, which ran from 2021 to 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties could be bought under the programme.

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel pleads for the Democratic Party to welcome more 'McCain-Romney Republicans'
articles.summary: Rahm Emanuel urged the Democratic Party to welcome "McCain-Romney Republicans" into their coalition, warning against far-left policies ahead of 2026 midterms.
articles.body: Former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel encouraged the Democratic Party to appeal to moderate "McCain-Romney Republicans" in an op-ed Wednesday. "The top story from the 2026 cycle will be the electoral opening Democrats seized — and will have to maintain," Emanuel wrote for The Wall Street Journal. "Most important, the McCain-Romney Republicans, who are politically homeless, need to be welcomed into Democrats’ governing and electoral coalition." Emanuel argued that moderate Republicans who associate their politics closer with former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney and former Arizona Sen. John McCain have been dissuaded from the GOP by President Donald Trump and could be the deciding factor in the 2026 midterm elections. LEE CARTER: 2026 ELECTION COULD ALL COME DOWN TO JUST ONE TYPE OF VOTER Romney and McCain were the last Republican nominees for president before Trump in 2012 and 2008, respectively, losing each time to Barack Obama. "Millions of McCain-Romney voters are redefining their political identities, and they will be most responsible for Democratic gains in November. These voters don’t want to be associated with MAGA, and they see themselves as free agents. The question for Democrats is whether we’re willing to give them a permanent home," Emanuel wrote. The former Clinton advisor pushed back on the idea that the Democratic Party should embrace the more extreme Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members, warning that the results of the midterm elections would be less a show of support for socialism than a rejection of "MAGA" politics. "The activists who reside in blue bubbles are sure to interpret the election results as vindication. But the party’s ascent won’t be born of some newfound enthusiasm for far-left policies such as defunding the police or offering free healthcare to illegal immigrants," Emanuel wrote. He added that Democrats should hesitate to impeach Trump and instead be focused on passing meaningful legislation, which is what moderate Republicans support as well. CARVILLE SAYS HE'D RATHER REPUBLICANS KEEP THE HOUSE THAN DEMOCRATS WIN BY FIVE SEATS, HELD 'HOSTAGE' BY DSA "Rather than vilifying those whose support we need, Democrats should be inviting them into our coalition. Voters willing to give Democrats a second look need convincing to trust us," Emanuel wrote. In a comment to Fox News Digital, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle defended Trump's record and encouraged all Republicans to double down on his agenda. "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress. The President signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs. The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction," Ingle said. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN' The Republican National Committee (RNC) also denied that Republicans could align themselves with the values of the Democratic Party. "Democrats are the party of abolishing private healthcare, defunding the police and hammering working families with higher taxes — those are not Republican values, or American values for that matter. If Democrats had their way, our country would look more like Caracas or Moscow," RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre told Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital reached out to the Democratic National Committee for comment. While speaking on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast earlier this month, Emanuel downplayed the impact the DSA candidates have on the Democratic Party as a whole. They believe in defunding the police, which is not the party position. They believe in open borders and open prisons. That's not the party’s position."

articles.title: Mom spots shipwreck hiding beneath lake after years of beach visits: 'Wait a minute'
articles.summary: Video shows the submerged remains of the A.H. Pitz, a 1923 tugboat discovered in Lake Superior's unusually clear waters by a Wisconsin camp director.
articles.body: A mother was enjoying a day at the beach recently with her 9-year-old son when the two of them unexpectedly stumbled upon a small piece of Midwestern history: a century-old shipwreck. Hannah Damon, director of outreach and administration at Camp Amnicon Adventures and Retreats in South Range, Wisconsin, made the discovery while spending time with her son along the camp's sandy shoreline. The shipwreck is the A.H. Pitz, a steam-powered tugboat built in 1923. It was abandoned in 1951. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER UNEXPECTED TWIST IN SHIPWRECK MYSTERY AFTER CLUES DON'T ADD UP Although Damon had known about the sunken vessel for years, she had never actually seen it until unusually clear water gave her and her son a rare glimpse of its remains. "We started seeing beams and cables and this massive pipe, and it was like, wait a minute, this is a shipwreck, this is a shipwreck," Damon told Fox News Digital on Thursday. Thrilled by the unexpected sighting, Damon rushed to grab her camera. "I ran back to shore and I got my camera, and I was like, OK, you are not allowed to splash me, this is a really exciting discovery," Damon recalled telling her son. UNDERWATER ROBOTICS EXPERT REVEALS 'SHIPWRECK CITY' HIDING BENEATH MAJOR URBAN LAKE Video taken by Damon shows the remains of the tugboat beneath clear water, with weathered wooden beams and other debris visible along the lakebed. Damon described the water as "crystal clear" and glassy, an unusual sight along that stretch of Lake Superior. The area sits within the Lake Superior clay plain, where the surrounding soil is largely composed of clay, which can make the water murky and obscure objects beneath the surface. Damon said the wreck is fully submerged and usually difficult to see. PARK RANGERS UNEARTH 200-YEAR-OLD SHIPWRECK ON REMOTE ISLAND DUBBED 'GRAVEYARD OF THE ATLANTIC' "I was actually just down back at the beach yesterday, and again, the water was calm, but it was murky again," Damon said. "I hope it's one of those things that, every once in a while, if you know where to look, you'll be able to find it. But it's definitely a rare find. It's really exciting." The A.H. Pitz was built in 1923 for the McMullen and Pitz Construction Company in Manitowoc, Wisconsin, and named after Armond Pitz, according to the Wisconsin Historical Society. The nearly 70-foot-long tugboat changed ownership several times before it was abandoned at the mouth of the Amnicon River in 1951. "It was really exciting to find it, to come across it, and I just couldn't wait to share it with the world." "I just couldn't wait to share it with the world." Damon later showed footage of the shipwreck on social media, where others shared their own memories of the vessel. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It was probably the closest thing to ‘viral’ the Camp Amnicon has ever experienced," Damon told Fox News Digital. Some commenters recalled seeing the vessel as far back as 1967, while others recognized its location along the Lake Superior shoreline. Damon said the response has helped reconnect members of the community through a shared piece of local history. articles.title: Saudi Arabia eyes bigger missiles as Houthi threat meets Iran nuclear fears
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities to produce larger, more powerful weapons, a development that could
articles.body: Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities to produce larger, more powerful weapons, a development that could strengthen its ability to strike targets across the region and intensify concerns over a potential nuclear arms race involving Iran.According to Reuters report, which cited an analysis of satellite imagery by US researchers, construction at a missile complex west of Riyadh points to a possible expansion of solid-fuel missile production. The researchers said the new facility could accommodate larger missile motors, potentially enabling the production of weapons with greater range or heavier payloads.The suspected expansion is centred on a ballistic missile complex at Al-Dawadmi, about 200 km west of Riyadh. Researchers Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute analysed commercial satellite images captured between April 2025 and September 2026, identifying a new building that appears to contain casting pits used to manufacture solid-fuel missile motors.The structure is at least twice the size of an existing facility, raising the possibility that it could support the production of larger missiles. The researchers said the complex could begin producing missiles by the end of 2026, depending on the installation of equipment.The expansion could also have implications for Saudi Arabia's confrontation with Yemen's Houthi movement, which has repeatedly used missiles and drones to target Saudi territory and regional interests.A larger domestic missile production capacity could give Riyadh greater flexibility in sustaining its arsenal and conducting retaliatory strikes. However, the satellite imagery does not establish the intended operational role of the new facility or confirm that production has begun.The researchers also assessed that Saudi Arabia may be producing Chinese-designed DF-15 ballistic missiles, pointing to footage they identified as showing the wreckage of a Saudi-fired DF-15 in Yemen.According to Reuters, the suspected missile programme could involve the DF-15 or a longer-range system similar to China's DF-21, although the precise missile type being manufactured at the expanded facility remains unconfirmed.If the assessment is correct, the development would point to a deeper Saudi reliance on Chinese missile technology as Riyadh seeks to strengthen its domestic defence industry.Saudi-Iran nuclear arms race fears growThe expansion of Saudi Arabia's ballistic missile programme is raising questions about the risk of a nuclear arms race with Iran, as Riyadh pursues a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Washington that would allow it to enrich uranium.The concern centres on whether more capable missiles could eventually serve as delivery systems for nuclear warheads if Saudi Arabia chose to pursue them. However, there is no public evidence establishing that the kingdom is currently developing nuclear weapons.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had said in a 2018 interview with CBS's 60 Minutes that Saudi Arabia would develop nuclear weapons if Iran acquired them.Reuters' July 22 report on the US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement also noted that the crown prince's statement has contributed to longstanding proliferation concerns surrounding the kingdom's nuclear ambitions.The nuclear issue has gained fresh attention following the US-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement announced on July 22. Reuters reported that the deal would allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium and reprocess nuclear waste, but would not require it to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, which gives inspectors broader powers to investigate potential undeclared nuclear activities.Saudi Arabia maintains that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes, while non-proliferation advocates have warned that enrichment and reprocessing technologies can provide pathways to weapons-usable material.The potential for a Saudi-Iran nuclear arms race remains conditional. Saudi Arabia's missile expansion and civilian nuclear plans do not prove that it is pursuing nuclear weapons, but its stated intention to match Iran if Tehran acquires a bomb has heightened concerns that a future Iranian nuclear weapon could trigger a wider regional proliferation crisis.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anti-terror police investigate as one person killed in shooting near Paris
articles.summary: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says the suspected gunman has been apprehended.
articles.body:
One person has been killed and four others wounded in a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which police have said they are treating as a terrorist incident.

Several drive-by shootings took place on Friday - first in Trappes to the southwest of Paris, and then nearby La Verrière - and a local mayor said a 12-year-old girl was among the wounded.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the suspected attacker had been "apprehended and placed in police custody".

The National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said it had taken on the investigation into the incident, which appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".

The mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.

The alleged gunman "wandered aimlessly" through several neighbourhoods and "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible", Rabeh told BFMTV. "He wanted to cause carnage," he said.

The mayor said he had targeted people at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before driving on to nearby La Verrière, where Mayor Nicolas Dainville said the four wounded were in critical condition.

A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town.

Asked what the motive for the shootings may have been, the mayor of Trappes said that the victim who had died was of African origin and one of those in a critical condition was of North African descent.

But in its own statement, the anti-terror prosecutor called for caution regarding the identity of the victims.

Among the alleged offences covered by the investigation, the prosecutor listed "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise" with the aggravated circumstance of acts committed because of "real or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnicity, nation or religion".

President Emmanuel Macron said: "Our thoughts go out to the victims, their families, as well as all the people of Yvelines. In this terrible ordeal, the nation stands by their side."

The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window.

A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two.

Rabeh said the shooter had hit a health centre, a petrol station and several vehicles during the spree.

The suspected attacker was then arrested at the nearby town of Coignières, local media report.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said en route to Trappes that the incident "looks like a murderous rampage" but that the motive of the attacker remained unclear.

The suspect, a 39-year-old, was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.

Rabeh suggested that the African heritage of two of the victims of the shooting may indicate a motive.

PNAT said their investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts.

The anti-terrorist office also said its investigation is looking into "conspiracy with a terrorist group for the purpose of preparing crimes against persons".

articles.title: Three fathers cleaned a neglected South Carolina creek for their children; a small clean-up drew 50 neighbours and sparked a wider wetland restoration movement
articles.summary: Three new fathers in Charleston, South Carolina, wanted their children to grow up with a closer connection to nature.
articles.body: Three new fathers in Charleston, South Carolina, wanted their children to grow up with a closer connection to nature. Their answer was to start with a neglected tidal creek near their homes, where rubbish had accumulated and the surrounding wetland faced pressure from development and urban runoff. In 2022, Joel Caldwell, Blake Scott and Blake Suárez organised a neighbourhood clean-up, expecting only a small group of volunteers. Instead, around 50 people turned up. The response encouraged the friends to expand their efforts beyond collecting rubbish. Through their initiative, known as the M.A.R.S.H. Project, they began protecting marshland, planting native vegetation, involving students in environmental monitoring and encouraging residents to care for Charleston's natural habitats.How three new South Carolina fathers started a conservation movementThe friends established the Marsh Appreciation and Restoration Society for Happiness, abbreviated as the M.A.R.S.H. Project, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Caldwell is a photographer and writer, Scott is a historian and international studies professor at the College of Charleston, and Suárez is a graphic designer.As new parents, they wanted their children to experience the natural world despite growing up in a developed urban neighbourhood. Halsey Creek, which runs through the Wagener Terrace neighbourhood, offered an opportunity to make that possible close to home.The founders initially expected a small group to join their first clean-up. Instead, around 50 volunteers arrived after Suárez helped publicise the event, showing the friends that other residents were keen to get involved in caring for the local environment.The clean-up that brought 50 neighbours togetherThe volunteers began removing rubbish that had accumulated along the creek. Over subsequent clean-ups, they retrieved tyres, radios, televisions and other discarded items. The work eventually included removing a car engine from the marsh with the help of winches.The initiative soon expanded beyond waste removal. The founders organised educational activities, public talks and planting events to help residents understand the ecosystem around them. They also encouraged neighbours to take part in conservation activities that could be carried out close to home.Why Halsey Creek matters to CharlestonHalsey Creek is a tidal salt marsh in Charleston's Wagener Terrace neighbourhood. It connects to the Ashley River and forms part of the city's remaining urban tidal creek ecosystem.Wetlands provide habitat for birds, fish, insects and plants, help filter some pollutants from water and can absorb and slow floodwater. These functions are particularly important in Charleston, a low-lying coastal city that faces tidal flooding and heavy rainfall.The creek supports wildlife in an increasingly developed urban landscape, with birds such as kingfishers and egrets observed around the marsh. However, a road crossing restricts tidal movement through part of the creek, while surrounding development and runoff place additional pressure on the waterway.The friends bought land to protect the marshOne of the project's significant steps was acquiring approximately one acre of land alongside Halsey Creek. The purchase was intended to prevent the parcel from being developed into housing and help preserve the marsh.The initiative has also involved planting native species, collecting native seeds and establishing pollinator gardens. The founders have encouraged residents to incorporate native vegetation into their own properties, creating additional habitat for insects and birds.In April 2023, the M.A.R.S.H. Project became a programme of the Carolina Ocean Alliance, a Charleston-based non-profit organisation working to protect, preserve and restore coastal ecosystems. The partnership provided an organisational base for the group's community activities and restoration efforts.Students and residents join the restoration effortThe project has expanded to involve residents, students and other local organisations. Activities have included citizen-science monitoring, water-quality testing, native-planting events and educational programmes. Students from the College of Charleston have also participated in internships and community outreach connected with the initiative.The founders are working towards a wider ecological corridor across the Charleston peninsula, encouraging residents to plant native species and preserve natural spaces so that habitats around different creeks become more connected.Their efforts have also contributed to discussions about Halsey Creek's future and ways to improve neighbourhood resilience. A watershed plan developed with scientists, students and other partners outlined nature-based approaches to flooding and ecological restoration. The work helped inform the City of Charleston's Halsey Creek Headwaters Masterplan, which addresses the area's ecological conditions and flood risks.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
