articles.title: US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
articles.summary: The positions of Washington and Tehran have changed dramatically since US-Israeli strikes began the war, analysts say.
articles.body:
Iran says seven oil tankers have caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz as its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warns that renewed US attacks could trigger a wider response and the world braces for the possibility of renewed hostilities .

Although analysts consider a US attack before the November 3 midterm elections unlikely, sabre-rattling on both sides has raised fears that escalating rhetoric could give way to renewed attacks with control of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian nuclear facilities at the heart of the conflict.

But the critical Gulf waterway, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped before the war, was not even an issue before the United States and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on February 28. Furthermore, talks over Iran’s nuclear programme were under way at the time.

As the US wrestles with depleted defensive weapons stocks and a global energy crisis mounts, how does the land lie now before potential renewed strikes and how does it differ from February before any of this began?

How has the geography of the war changed?

Unlike in February before the war began, the US and Iran would be fighting it out on several different fronts if attacks resume.

While the objective of US-Israeli strikes on Iran was initially to topple its leadership, another aim was to weaken Iran’s regional allies, including Hamas and Hezbollah. Announcing the offensive, Trump pledged to prevent Tehran-backed groups from attacking US forces and destabilising the region.

While the offensive failed to force a change in Iran’s government, Hamas has been severely weakened as Israel continues to attack Gaza – with more than 1,400 Palestinians killed since a US-backed “ceasefire” was announced in October last year.

Hezbollah’s retaliation against targets in northern Israel after the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the first US-Israeli air strikes brought Lebanon into the war in early March.

Israel launched a bombing campaign against sites in southern Lebanon and the suburbs of Beirut it considers Hezbollah strongholds and, at one point, occupied about one-fifth of the country, displacing more than one million people. It still occupies significant land on Lebanon’s southern border.

Waterways, energy facilities now battlegrounds

The biggest geographical change, however, has been the emergence of the Gulf’s waterways and energy infrastructure as key targets. Iranian attacks on US military assets and civilian infrastructure have exposed Gulf countries to the consequences of a war they had hoped to avoid.

Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera: “US-Iran negotiations had previously centred on Iran’s regional allies and nuclear programme. The Strait of Hormuz and attacks on the Gulf have now become central points of contention.”

While the Gulf has experienced attacks before, Coningham said the scale and “velocity” of recent Iranian strikes, including on oil and gas infrastructure, have marked a significant shift.

The Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman, which had been freely open to international shipping before the war, now gives Tehran a means of imposing costs far beyond its borders. Iran continues to threaten and attack shipping there while the US maintains its own blockade of Iranian ports. Traffic has been severely disrupted and supplies of oil and gas have been sharply reduced.

In March, CNN reported that the Pentagon and US National Security Council had significantly underestimated Iran’s willingness to restrict passage through the strait and the consequences of that. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected the reporting, insisting the military had planned for that possibility.

Renewed fighting between the forces of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government of Yemen and the Iran-backed Houthis has added another front to the regional crisis. Yemen’s war has expanded to Saudi Arabia as Houthi missile and drone attacks target Saudi airports and oil infrastructure.

This front has brought another trade chokepoint into sharper focus – Bab al-Mandeb, the strait that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping there could compound transportation disruptions in Hormuz, undermine efforts to move Gulf exports through alternative routes and place additional pressure on the US.

The two countries’ leaders face different constraints. Iran’s rulers remain concerned about unrest and their own survival but do not face the same electoral reckoning as Trump’s Republican Party, which faces midterm elections in less than two weeks.

Before the February strikes, Iran’s government faced deep public anger after its deadly crackdown in January on nationwide protests against high inflation and the plummeting value of Iran’s currency. US-Israeli attacks subsequently killed Khamenei, who had ruled since 1989, and security chief Ali Larijani. But they did not topple the Islamic Republic.

Khamenei’s son Mojtaba succeeded him. His elevation and the influence of the IRGC has reinforced the position of hardliners within the government.

Coningham cautioned that the absence of demonstrations during a war should not be interpreted as support for the government.

“While the conflict had produced a rallying effect around resistance to foreign attacks, that did not mean Iran had emerged stronger,” he said.

Meanwhile, Trump faces much tougher political pressure before any renewed strikes. His approval rating has fallen from 40 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll reported days before the war began to just 31 percent in a survey released on Monday – the lowest recorded by the pollster across either of Trump’s presidential terms – amid frustration over high petrol prices and the deep unpopularity of the war on Iran among Americans.

Iran’s economy was already struggling before the war, weighed down by sanctions and assets frozen abroad. The conflict has deepened those pressures as the US combines military force, more sanctions and a naval blockade to squeeze the country further.

In April, Iran’s government estimated the direct and indirect damage from US-Israeli attacks at $270bn. The pressure intensified in late August when Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast , seeking to isolate Iran from international trade by imposing penalties on those doing business with it.

Official figures showed Iran’s gross domestic product contracted by 10.1 percent year-on-year from March 21 to June 20. Energy exports have been severely curtailed by the US blockade while the rial has plunged in value.

The US has also incurred substantial costs. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the conflict had cost the Department of Defense $38bn as of August 1. It said continued operations were expected to cost about $2bn to $3bn a month, depending on the intensity of fighting.

As a result of the additional costs of the war, US government debt surpassed a record $40 trillion in August – two years before it had been expected to reach that level.

While the US has demonstrated its ability to strike deep inside Iran, that destructive capacity has not brought down Iran’s political system nor has it finished off Tehran’s ability to retaliate with strikes on US assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries.

Coningham said the difficulty for Washington is “translating military superiority into strategic results”. He also described recent troop redeployments as possible military posturing, but he added that the deployments do represent a shift from earlier efforts to reduce the US military footprint in parts of the region.

US media reports suggested there is now a severe shortage of weapons in the US arsenal in the Middle East as expensive defensive missiles have been depleted against a bombardment of cheap Iranian drones.

Fox News reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit were expected to reach the Middle East by the end of November, bringing about 10,000 military personnel. The deployment would expand Trump’s military options as he weighs further action.

Coningham said, for Iran, the conflict fits a longstanding narrative of resistance against what its leadership portrayed as US and Israeli colonialism and imperialism.

Since February 28, the IRGC has demonstrated its skill at “asymmetric warfare” as it has held off expensive US military might with cheap, mass-produced drones.

Furthermore, its use of “decentralised structures” has allowed it to continue operating despite disrupted communications and the loss of senior decision-makers, Coningham said.

US strikes have severely damaged Iran’s navy and increased its reliance on smaller vessels, including speedboats used in recent attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. On that front, geography is on Iran’s side as it can fire at ships in the Strait of Hormuz from ground positions along its coast. It can also place sea mines in the strait using rockets to drop them .

These are tactics the US had not necessarily expected to contend with when it initiated the strikes on Iran but will certainly face now.

A mounting global energy crisis was not on the cards in February, but it is certainly looming now.

Disruptions to Gulf energy supplies caused by the war and fears of further escalation have pushed oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began.

It hit $126.41 on April 30, its highest level in four years. By early trading on Friday, it stood at $114.47.

But the crisis extends beyond crude oil . Damage and disruptions to fuel production in the Middle East alongside sanctions on Russian supplies have tightened diesel markets while the global supply of liquefied natural gas has also been heavily affected. The International Energy Agency warned in October that supply constraints could persist well into 2027.

Diesel, which has doubled in price in the US, is a big problem for Trump because farmers and businesses in the US, key voting blocs for him, rely on it for production and transport.

Alternative ports, pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers have helped Gulf producers restore exports but at higher logistical costs and with continuing exposure to attacks.

Re-establishing shipping through vital waterways in the Middle East, therefore, has now become a primary objective in the war.

articles.title: Denmark nurdles may be from River Tyne spill, says Danish environment agency
articles.summary: The Danish Environment Protection Agency says nurdles it has tested are similar to the Tyne pellets.
articles.body:
Nurdles found along the Danish coast are likely to originate from the spill in north-east England, according to the country's environment agency.

Masses of plastic pellets were found along the western coast of Denmark in September.

The Danish Environment Protection Agency has now confirmed tests carried out on the microplastics suggest they originated from the River Tyne spill in August.

It said the nurdles had the same characteristics as the one billion which had been spilled in north-east England and their arrival in Denmark in late September and early October was consistent with "current patterns and circulation in the North Sea".

Signe Simonsen, the head of startup Race for Oceans Technology, first spotted the nurdles on the island of Mandø in Denmark on 26 September.

"There were just so many milk white plastic pellets," she said. "So many that I've never seen before in this area."

Simonsen said the discovery of the nurdles had made her "really sad" considering the "pristine" nature of the Wadden Sea.

Simonsen then said she drove along the coast of several nearby islands which are roughly on the same latitude as Newcastle.

She said there were nurdles "all over" where the tide had washed up.

Simonsen said she had collected nurdles from 10 different spots along the Danish coast and Sylt in Germany.

Simonsen, whose firm aims to detect microplastic pollution from drone images, then passed on some of her samples to the Danish Environment Protection Agency.

The agency, which tested the pellets alongside Aarhus University, said another factor which suggested the Danish nurdles were the same as those spilled in the River Tyne was the fact there were no other recorded spills in the area that could explain their presence.

Nurdles from the spill have washed up along the coast of north-east England including Teesside and Durham.

As of September, about 28% of the nurdles are believed to have been recovered.

articles.title: Jersey inflation rate rises to 3%, figures show
articles.summary: The rising cost of food and alcohol drives an increase in the inflation rate, figures show.
articles.body:
The annual rate of inflation in Jersey rose to 3% in September, according to new figures.

Jersey's retail price index (RPI) rose 0.2 percentage points since June when it was 2.8%.

Statistics Jersey said increases in the cost of household services, alcoholic drinks and food made the most notable contributions to annual rate of inflation.

It said there were also "substantial increases" in the price of some fuels, with heating oil and other fuels increasing by 47.7% across the year, while petrol and oil increased by 22.7%. It said food prices increased by 3.5% and housing costs by 0.2%.

Statistics Jersey said this quarter the island's headline inflation rate was 0.6 percentage points lower than the UK's CPIH, a measure of inflation that includes housing costs, which stood at 3.6%.

It said housing costs made the largest contribution to the RPI - this group includes public and private rentals, as well as mortgage interest payments, parish rates and maintenance and repair costs.

Statisticians said global energy markets remained affected by conflict in the Middle East.

articles.title: In the early 1800s, a Pennsylvania artist painted George Washington and a 13-star eagle on a bookplate; after over 60 years in a private collection, it emerged from a manila folder and sold for $226,600
articles.summary: A rare early 19th-century Pennsylvania Dutch folk art drawing showing George Washington and an American eagle with 13 stars has sold at auction for
articles.body: A rare early 19th-century Pennsylvania Dutch folk art drawing showing George Washington and an American eagle with 13 stars has sold at auction for $226,600 (£175,000). The artwork had remained hidden in a plain manila folder for more than six decades. The double-page ink and watercolour fraktur bookplate was made in Pennsylvania in the early 1800s. According to auction details published by Pook & Pook Inc., the piece came from a private collection where it had remained untouched inside a folder for more than 60 years. Bidding at the auction house's salesroom in Downingtown, Pennsylvania, far exceeded the original estimate of $15,000 to $25,000. The artwork eventually sold for $226,600, including the buyer's premium.Rediscovery of a hidden folk art treasureFraktur is a distinctive folk art tradition that Pennsylvania German settlers practised from the mid-18th century to the mid-19th century. These works were usually made with ink and watercolour on paper. They often appeared in family Bibles, birth certificates and religious books as decorative bookplates or pages used to record important details. The recently sold piece features a detailed design spread across two pages, painted with bright colours. One side shows a full-length portrait of George Washington. The other features an American bald eagle surrounded by 13 stars, representing the original American colonies. In its report on the sale, Antiques & The Arts Weekly noted that the artwork attracted strong competition from bidders on the phone and online. Its excellent condition and rare patriotic images helped drive interest. The artwork had stayed inside a dark paper folder for more than six decades. This protected the original ink and watercolour from sunlight and helped preserve its bright colours.Artistic context and historical linksArt historians connect the style of the work to the Schwenkfelder folk art traditions of Southeastern Pennsylvania. Reference material cited in the lot catalogue by Pook & Pook points to similar historical works recorded in Fraktur Writings and Folk Art Drawings of the Schwenkfelder Library Collection by Dennis Moyer. Many surviving fraktur drawings mainly feature flowers, birds or religious messages. Political and patriotic figures, such as George Washington, appear much less often. Showing the first US president alongside national symbols gave early German-speaking immigrants a way to express their sense of belonging and civic identity in the young American republic. The final price of $226,600 places the artwork among the most valuable fraktur pieces sold at public auction in recent years.Strong demand for American folk artThe sale reflects continued demand for high-quality objects linked to Pennsylvania German culture and history. Collectibles with a clear ownership history and original colours continue to attract strong prices from specialist folk art collectors and American historical institutions. According to post-sale data released by Pook & Pook, the auction house attracted wide interest across its entire Americana catalogue. The patriotic fraktur was the event's top lot. All hammer prices from the sale reflect final transactions that include buyer's premiums, as recorded by the auction house.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: From ghats to gated communities: How faith tourism is reshaping Haridwar’s real estate
articles.summary: India’s domestic tourism sector is experiencing a dramatic transformation, with spiritual and pilgrimage tourism as the major growth driver.
articles.body: India’s domestic tourism sector is experiencing a dramatic transformation, with spiritual and pilgrimage tourism as the major growth driver. A market that has been largely niche has turned into a larger consumer trend, changing travel patterns and real estate development. Haridwar, the gateway city to the Char Dham circuit, is at the epicenter of this change, data shows there is substantial demand growth and infrastructure constraints. Dr. Annkit A Jayant, Founder & CEO, HP Global Infrra shares insights.The demand expansionThe recent travel data on Cleartrip's PeekABoo Trends Tracker shows clear and tangible evidence of this change. Haridwar’s hotel bookings increased 161 percent year-on-year with bus bookings up 203 percent. The Char Dham circuit more broadly has similar trends of growth as well (Rishikesh saw 113 percent growth in bus bookings, and Varanasi, Prayagraj, and Ayodhya saw triple-digit growth in accommodation). With the growth rate of accommodation bookings far exceeding the capacity of hotels, this is influencing pricing and asset utilization.Shifting demographicsThe composition of spiritual tourism's audience has broadened considerably. Pilgrimage travel was historically concentrated among older age groups and family units, but now attracts younger professionals, independent travelers, and notably, solo women travelers. Flight bookings among solo women travelers increased 20 percent year-on-year during the Amarnath Yatra season. Hotel bookings during this period rose 22 percent, and bus bookings surged 104 percent. Dwarka recorded 37 percent growth from solo women travelers.This demographic expansion carries practical implications for accommodation design. The traditional family-oriented model is insufficient to serve travelers with distinct preferences regarding safety, privacy, and service infrastructure. The diversification of traveler profiles requires differentiated accommodation products serving varying preference spectrums.Budget and mid-market growthHousing trends are evident in budget and mid-range accommodation segments. Budget hotel bookings increased 386 percent year-on-year and mid-range properties 164 percent. This divergence from luxury expansion indicates that demand in price-conscious and aspirational middle-class segments is more concentrated than in luxury areas. Budget accommodation is still underbuilt in comparison to demand, especially in gateway cities. Rishikesh, Haridwar, and other Char Dham points have seen much higher booking growth in lower-priced rooms as existing inventory is not filling all the need. Mid-range properties also show a gap between available inventory and demand, resulting in distinct operational margins and utilization profiles.Geographic demand patternsTravelers booking Haridwar trips predominantly originate from India's major metropolitan centers-Bengaluru, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Delhi, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai, and Ahmedabad. This concentration indicates pilgrimage demand increasingly originates from urban, economically active populations with disposable income and time flexibility. This demand pattern reflects urbanization dynamics and rising middle-class travel participation rather than cyclical trends. As urban centers expand and disposable income rises, the addressable market for spiritual tourism grows correspondingly. The geographic concentration enables more predictable market segmentation and targeted capacity planning.Seasonal architecturePilgrimage destinations fall on different demand calendars due to festival cycles. Puri’s Jagannath Rath Yatra brought in over 200 per cent more hotel bookings. Mathura saw 196 per cent growth during Guru Purnima and Govardhan Parikrama seasons. Varanasi grew 161 per cent during Sawan and Kanwar Yatra.The demand structure of Haridwar is different because there are many pilgrimage seasons and festivals and their visitations are all year round, the Char Dham season, Maha Kumbh cycle and various festivals are all accompanied by peak demand. Such multi-wave demand architecture offers more distributed revenue streams and less seasonal cash flow volatility than single-event destinations. The calendar-driven demand provides easy capacity planning as well as resource allocation, unlike discretionary leisure tourism that is cyclical.Capacity-demand misalignmentThe data indicates structural misalignment between capacity and demand. Booking growth rates of 161 to 203 percent vastly exceed typical accommodation supply expansion rates of 5 to 15 percent annually. New facility development typically requires 18 to 36 months from planning to operation, meaning demand currently outpaces supply timelines. This mismatch creates elevated pricing in existing inventory while new entrants assess price sustainability.The traveler composition, increasingly budget and mid-range oriented—suggests demand exists at price points where construction costs and land economics remain viable, potentially enabling continued development activity.Operational flexibilityBeyond traditional room rentals, accommodation operators can develop supplementary revenue streams. Corporate retreats and wellness programming during off-peak periods, cultural and educational tourism overlays, and experiential services could enhance utilization rates and stabilize cash flow. Location within Haridwar remains material proximity to pilgrimage sites and transportation infrastructure influence facility performance substantially.Haridwar's real estate market reflects demonstrable shifts in domestic travel patterns. Current evidence suggests demand expansion continues exceeding supply development, with demographic broadening occurring across multiple pilgrimage circuits. Understanding these underlying demand dynamics remains essential for informed decision-making regarding development timing and positioning.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Around 1929, Albert Einstein filled a handwritten letter to mathematician Chaim Herman Muntz with equations; nearly a century later, the one-page document and its original envelope sold for $71,811
articles.summary: A handwritten letter in which Albert Einstein explained a mathematical problem to a fellow researcher nearly 100 years ago has sold for $71,811 at an
articles.body: A handwritten letter in which Albert Einstein explained a mathematical problem to a fellow researcher nearly 100 years ago has sold for $71,811 at an auction. The document, believed to have been mailed around 1929, contains a page of equations and notes addressed to mathematician Chaim Herman Muntz. It was sold by RR Auction last week, along with the original envelope in which it had been sent from Germany.According to the auction house, the letter offers a look at a scientific discussion between Einstein and Muntz during the late 1920s. Written in German and signed "A. Einstein", the document measures 8.75 by 11 inches. Its exact date is unknown, but the envelope carries a postmark from Potsdam, Germany, apparently dating to 1929. The auction house had placed an estimate of $20,000 or more on the letter, which eventually sold for $71,811, including the buyer's premium.The letter concerns Hamiltonian mechanics, a mathematical method used in classical physics to study the motion of physical systems. Einstein was examining whether certain mathematical relationships would continue to hold when the equations describing them were transformed. His explanation takes up almost the entire page.A scientific discussion that began years earlierEinstein and Muntz had been corresponding since 1927, well before the letter was apparently mailed. Their exchanges involved mathematical questions connected to Einstein's research, including his efforts to bring different physical forces into a single theoretical framework.By 1928, the two were discussing distant parallelism, also called Fernparallelismus. Einstein was investigating this mathematical approach as part of his attempt to develop a unified theory of gravitation and electromagnetism.Muntz contributed calculations to that work, particularly on a problem involving central symmetry. Einstein later acknowledged his contribution in published research.The collaboration continued while Einstein was developing his ideas about a unified field theory. Between 1928 and 1931, he produced several papers using distant parallelism. In 1929, Hamilton's principle also became relevant to this research as he considered mathematical questions raised by Muntz and Cornelius Lanczos.However, the newly sold letter does not appear to deal directly with the unified-field theory. RR Auction's description indicates that Einstein was examining a different problem involving the mathematical behaviour of equations in classical mechanics.What do the equations in the letter mean?At the centre of Einstein's calculations are two concepts: covariance and invariance. Both concern what happens to mathematical expressions when the variables or mathematical descriptions used in a problem are changed.Invariance means that a particular mathematical expression remains unchanged under a specified transformation. Covariance, meanwhile, concerns how mathematical relationships behave when such transformations are made.Einstein wanted to establish which relationships in the problem would retain the required mathematical properties. To do this, he used Hamilton's canonical equations, which are part of Hamiltonian mechanics. These equations describe how certain quantities associated with a physical system change over time.The question was not simply whether an equation could be written differently. Einstein was examining the mathematical conditions under which its relationships would remain valid.He considered transformations that preserve a particular expression and used that condition to establish further results. One conclusion provided the basis for another, allowing him to determine the properties of a more complicated equation.The handwritten page also contains a correction. Einstein crossed out the word "covariant" and replaced it with "invariant" while discussing one of the mathematical expressions.By the end of the letter, he appeared satisfied that the equation met the conditions he had been investigating. "We probably cannot demand more than that," Einstein wrote. He then proposed using the equation to study what he called "the problem of the rotator".Why the letter attracted attention at auctionThe document is unusual because it contains an extended mathematical explanation rather than a brief message or a simple statement of Einstein's conclusions.Bobby Livingston, executive vice president at RR Auction, said the letter allows readers to see how Einstein developed his calculations.“What's interesting about this letter is that you can follow Einstein's calculations across the entire page,” Livingston said, as quoted by Fine Books and Collection. “He's working through the mathematics, explaining his reasoning to a fellow mathematician and suggesting what they should investigate next. You can see the progression of his thinking right on the page,” he added.Einstein's letter was one of several historical items offered in RR Auction's Fine Autographs and Artifacts sale. A document signed by King Edward IV fetched $37,535, while another bearing King Henry VIII's signature sold for $33,901.An autograph scrapbook containing signatures of prominent figures, including Babe Ruth, Amelia Earhart and Thomas Edison, fetched $28,759.You use AI every day. border battalion as the force strengthens its combat readiness along the 3,488-km Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The ITBP chief’s remarks came as the force steps up its modernisation drive, with a greater focus on emerging warfare technologies and specialised training.Addressing personnel at an ITBP base in Alwar, Rajasthan, ahead of the force’s 65th Raising Day on October 24, Kapoor said traditional methods of warfare were no longer sufficient to counter China, which he described as India’s “biggest adversary”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 6 ancient Ayurvedic remedies thar are making a comeback in women's wellness
articles.summary: Women's wellness has never had more information, products or protocols. Yet, paradoxically, many women I speak with describe feeling increasingly depleted.
articles.body: Women's wellness has never had more information, products or protocols. Yet, paradoxically, many women I speak with describe feeling increasingly depleted. They may be eating better and exercising, but still experience low energy, poor sleep, stress, digestive discomfort, bloating, or simply a persistent sense of not feeling their best. I call this modern-life depletion.Our bodies were not designed around 12-hour screen exposure, irregular meals, fragmented sleep, sedentary routines, environmental stressors and the mental load of being constantly "on." And the effects rarely stay confined to one part of the body. Stress affects sleep. Sleep influences metabolism and recovery. Digestion affects how nutrients are absorbed. Hormonal rhythms interact with stress and metabolic health.This is where I believe Ayurveda's resurgence becomes interesting. Its relevance isn't simply about rediscovering old herbs. It is about rediscovering a systems approach to wellbeing.Here are six Ayurvedic remedies and practices finding renewed relevance in women's wellness.1. Shatavari: Few Ayurvedic herbs are as closely associated with women as Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus). Traditionally regarded as a nourishing rasayana, it has long been used across different stages of a woman's life. Today, interest is growing alongside more open conversations around menstruation, perimenopause, menopause and healthy ageing. Its naturally occurring compounds include steroidal saponins known as shatavarins, along with flavonoids and polysaccharides.But I believe its modern relevance is best understood beyond the idea of a "hormonal herb." Hormonal wellbeing doesn't exist independently of stress, sleep, nutrition and metabolism. Shatavari represents a broader shift toward supporting women through physiological transitions rather than chasing a quick fix for individual symptoms.2. Ashwagandha: Perhaps no Ayurvedic concept feels more contemporary than resilience. Many women move continuously between professional responsibility, caregiving, family and an almost invisible mental workload. The body may stop working at the end of the day; the mind often doesn't.Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) has traditionally been associated with restoration, vitality and resilience, and modern research has increasingly examined it in relation to stress response, sleep and cognitive wellbeing. That matters because chronic stress is not simply an emotional experience; it can influence sleep, appetite, digestion, energy, recovery and hormonal signalling. Ashwagandha's modern relevance, then, may be less about "reducing stress" and more about supporting the body's capacity to adapt and recover from it.3. Triphala: Ayurveda placed extraordinary importance on digestion long before "gut health" became a global wellness category. Triphala, traditionally combining Amalaki, Bibhitaki and Haritaki, has been used to support digestion and elimination, and it feels particularly relevant now, when routines include irregular meals, processed foods, stress eating, inadequate fibre, frequent travel and prolonged sitting.We often focus on what we eat. But nutrition is only as useful as the body's ability to digest, absorb, utilise and eliminate. The modern gut conversation increasingly connects digestive health with metabolic and immune function; Ayurveda approached this differently, but the underlying systems perspective is strikingly familiar.4. Punarnava: Bloating and puffiness are familiar experiences for many women, particularly during hormonal fluctuations, travel and periods of inactivity. Punarnava (Boerhavia diffusa) has traditionally been used in Ayurveda in relation to fluid balance and natural elimination pathways.What interests me about Punarnava is the larger principle it represents. Fluid balance isn't simply about "getting rid of water." It reflects coordinated physiological processes involving kidney function, circulation, electrolytes and metabolism. In an industry often focused on aggressive detoxes and cleanses, Ayurveda offers another perspective: support the systems the body already uses to filter, release and rebalance.5. Turmeric: Few Ayurvedic ingredients have made a comeback quite like turmeric (Curcuma longa). For generations, haldi existed somewhere between food, household wisdom and traditional care. Today, modern interest centres largely on curcuminoids, particularly curcumin, and their antioxidant and inflammatory-response properties, making turmeric relevant to conversations around cellular wellbeing, recovery, metabolic wellness and healthy ageing.Yet turmeric also illustrates a limitation of the modern wellness industry: we sometimes isolate one "hero ingredient" and expect it to compensate for an unhealthy system. No herb can fully offset persistent sleep deprivation, chronic stress, inadequate nutrition and inactivity. The ingredient matters. The biological environment around it matters too.6. Abhyanga: Perhaps the most interesting Ayurvedic comeback is not something we consume at all. Abhyanga, the traditional practice of gently massaging the body with warm oil, is one of Ayurveda's oldest daily rituals.A small pilot study examining daily 30-minute Abhyanga over 15 days reported a 16.4% reduction in perceived stress scores and a nearly 28% improvement in sleep-disturbance scores. These preliminary findings shouldn't be read as definitive evidence, but they make this ancient practice particularly interesting through the lens of modern stress and recovery research. Massage and therapeutic touch are also being explored more broadly for their effect on relaxation and the autonomic nervous system.For me, Abhyanga represents something bigger. Modern wellness repeatedly asks women: What else should you take? What else should you track? What else should you optimize? Ayurveda sometimes asks the opposite: can you slow down enough to let the body recover?The bigger comeback is systems thinkingWhat interests me most about the return of these remedies isn't nostalgia for ancient medicine. It is the return of a fundamental idea: the body does not operate in silos. Stress, sleep, digestion, metabolism, hormonal rhythms, elimination and recovery continuously influence one another. This thinking shaped my own journey, and eventually, the philosophy behind Ubalance Naturals: support the systems rather than chase individual symptoms. Ayurveda should not replace appropriate medical care, nor should ancient remedies be turned into modern miracle claims. Their real relevance may be far more valuable than that.In a world constantly asking women to do more, perhaps wellness begins by asking a different question: what is modern life continuously depleting, and what does the body need to restore its capacity for balance? That, to me, is where ancient wisdom and modern women's wellness meaningfully meet.By Gurmeet Kaur, Co-Founder, Ubalance Naturals

Ukraine said it recaptured more of its territory than Russia had managed to seize this year, despite restrictions on US satellite services critical to its defence.

Russia responded by hitting dozens of Ukraine’s energy facilities and using cluster bombs in attacks that harmed civilians.

“Our soldiers have liberated more territory since the beginning of autumn than the Russians have managed to capture,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a public address.

Ukrainian General Staff spokesman Andriy Kovalev denied Russian claims to have seized 1,800 sq km (700 square miles) of Ukrainian territory during the autumn.

The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank that uses geolocated open-source information to assess territorial movements, said Ukraine had made a net gain of 241 sq km (93 square miles) since September 1, effectively eliminating any Russian territorial gains this year.

Russia’s casualties suggest the effectiveness of its forces is in decline.

Russian losses – meaning those killed or severely wounded – hovered around 30,000 a month from January to May, but steadily increased over the summer. According to Ukrainian estimates, Russia lost 46,230 soldiers in September, its highest monthly losses of the year, and 37,000 so far in October.

October 21 marked its highest daily losses of the entire war, at 2,250, said Robert Brovdi, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine, as his unit’s kill rate had climbed to a new record.

Overall, Ukraine estimated there were more than 350,000 Russian dead and wounded since the beginning of the year.

Many of Ukraine’s territorial gains were made by Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counteroffensive that stopped a Russian pincer movement to recapture the remaining one-fifth of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region – roughly 5,500 sq km (2,000 square miles).

General Andriy Biletskyi, who led Ukraine’s Third Army Corps to victory in that campaign, said he had eliminated a Russian bridgehead on the western bank of the Zherebets river, and crossed over to the east bank, shortening his own front line and concentrating artillery and unmanned aerial firepower, stabilising its defence.

The defeat of the pincer, said Biletskyi, had left Russia with the unsavoury option of a frontal assault on the “fortress belt” of heavily defended cities of Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and Druzhivka.

Russia had “temporarily abandoned this plan, although it plans to resume it,” Biletskyi told the Ukrainian news outlet Suspilne. Russian military expert Andrey Marochko told Russia’s state news agency TASS that Ukraine was reinforcing the fortress cities.

Russia has responded to its sagging military fortunes by increasing the ferocity of its attacks on civilians.

On October 22, it flew three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads into Kyiv, Zelenskyy said.

“This warhead detonates above the ground and is specifically designed to inflict maximum damage on people and equipment within an area of 400 by 400 metres,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry senior adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov . “45 submunitions explode in the air.”

One of the warheads struck an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra cathedral and a monastery.

“There was not even theoretically any military object nearby,” said Zelenskyy. “It is a deliberate choice of weapons, a deliberate choice of the area.”

Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed it had targeted an assembly building for the FP-5 long-range drones and FP-9 missiles Ukraine has been using against it, as well as other drone manufacturing sites.

More than anything else, though, Russia has relentlessly targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, despite United States President Donald Trump declaring an energy ceasefire for both sides on October 11.

Since then, there had been more than 170 strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy said.

“Russia is not achieving any significant results on the front lines. Therefore, it is directing all its aggression and hatred towards terrorising civilian infrastructure: electricity, heating, and now, water. The goal is clear – to exhaust the people,” Prime Minister Serhiy Khoretskyi told the BBC.

Since he assumed office on July 16, he said, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure 2,147 times.

Ukraine has been hampered in its defence by the US, which on October 8 was understood to have stopped providing early warning of incoming ballistic missiles for the second time this year.

Zelenskyy said that early warning had been restored on October 20, but three other US actions detrimental to Ukraine’s defence had not been reversed.

One was Trump’s waiver of oil export sanctions on Russia to lower the price of diesel, which he formalised with an executive order on October 16. Putin said on October 21 that Russia’s first shipment of 40,000 tonnes of diesel to the US would depart within two or three days.

Another issue was that the US has not released Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, which are its most effective defence against ballistic missiles, despite having previously supplied a dozen a month, and despite the fact that Europe has paid for them.

But the biggest problem was that Ukraine’s ability to fly its drones at more than 150kmh (100mph) using the Starshield satellite navigation system remained suspended.

Ukraine has said it cannot intercept fast-moving jet-powered drones at such speeds, and its attacks on Russian logistics, as well as the resupply of its own front lines by drone, are also rendered more vulnerable.

Starshield was created as a military application of Starlink, owned by Elon Musk, and he and the White House traded blame for making the decision to restrict it throughout the week. Trump said on October 22 that Starlink and Starshield services were about to be restored.

After initially observing Trump’s energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed targeting Russian energy infrastructure, as part of an economic strategy to starve the Russian war machine of export revenue.

On October 18, it struck the St Petersburg oil terminal, Russia’s biggest offloading terminal for oil exports. It also hit a data centre serving Russian social media platform Vkontakte, disrupting services.

Other facilities were likely targeted. Russia’s Defence Ministry said it had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over various regions that night.

The US appeared to leverage its waiver of diesel sanctions and the suspension of Starshield services to push for a trilateral meeting among the US, Russia and Ukraine.

US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo on October 20, and followed up with a meeting with Putin in St Petersburg the following day.

Putin aide Yuri Ushakov told the media that Russia had agreed “in principle” to meet on November 10. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the planned meeting would be held in Abu Dhabi.

articles.title: Hundreds to defy Palestine Action ban in protest at US embassy in London
articles.summary: Campaigners plan mass Halloween action before Supreme Court hearing on challenge to group’s ‘terrorist’ proscription.
articles.body:
More than 400 people are expected to gather outside the United States embassy in London on October 31 in the latest act of mass defiance against the British government’s ban on the Palestine Action group.

Protesters plan to hold placards reading: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” and campaign group Defend Our Juries said a parallel action will take place outside the US consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland.

More than 3,850 people have been arrested for publicly backing Palestine Action since the United Kingdom’s government proscribed it as a “terrorist” organisation in July 2025, Defend Our Juries said.

The timing of the demonstrations is calculated. In June, the Court of Appeal sided with the government and overturned a High Court ruling that had found the proscription unlawful.

On November 4 and 5, the UK Supreme Court will hear an appeal by Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori.

Among those Al Jazeera spoke to at the group’s previous action outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court was Teresa, a former teacher-turned-activist who has been arrested multiple times for protesting against the proscription.

“It’s a badge of honour , to be able to do this for Gaza” she told Al Jazeera.

She is not alone. Those arrested at recent actions include Massive Attack’s Rob del Naja, 94-year-old human rights barrister Margaret Owen, former government adviser Jonathan Porritt and the Reverend Sue Parfitt.

Organisers want to raise the possibility that the UK move to ban Palestine Action came under pressure from US President Donald Trump.

The proscription followed an incident in which activists spray-painted Trump’s Turnberry golf course in Scotland. The US president labelled the action “terrorism” on his Truth Social platform and praised then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s response.

During the legal challenge, it emerged that Trump and Starmer had spoken by phone twice about Palestine Action in March 2025. Starmer had requested updates from Police Scotland on the arrests and briefed Trump on developments.

The US president’s son Eric Trump also met Scottish First Minister John Swinney before the ban was announced, and documents released under the Freedom of Information Act showed the Turnberry protest was discussed.

The Halloween protests will also come three days after a hearing in the trial of the Turnberry protesters at the High Court in Glasgow. Prosecutors are now seeking to have the seven defendants sentenced as “terrorists”, a move critics called “completely disproportionate”.

The same week that the prosecutors made that call, Washington designated Palestine Action a “terrorist organisation”.

Defend Our Juries said the resulting sanctions have blocked Ammori from crowdfunding for her Supreme Court challenge.

This week, actors Paul Mescal, Jessie Buckley and Susan Sarandon along with broadcaster Gary Lineker signed a letter published on the cover of the New Statesman magazine urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government to drop the “draconian” legislation.

Campaigners said the ban on the group has also in effect halted UK sales of books by the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, a Palestine Action supporter.

However, when author Sarah Helm, wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, publicly declared her support for Palestine Action, the Metropolitan Police took no action. Defend Our Juries said that exposes a ban that cannot be enforced evenly.

Shami Chakrabarti, a senior figure in the ruling Labour Party, has urged the home secretary to lift the ban.

Speaking to the LBC radio station, the former shadow attorney general said it “makes a mockery” of counterterrorism law and the power to proscribe should be exceptional and kept under constant review.

“I’d better be careful what I say, or I’ll be arrested,” she added.

The government argued that Palestine Action’s campaign of break-ins and criminal damage at defence sites, including those linked to Israeli arms maker Elbit Systems, meets the legal threshold for proscription. The Court of Appeal described it as a covert organisation operating through secret cells.

Defend Our Juries insisted its own protests are entirely peaceful.

“This mass defiance and the mass arrests expected to follow will lay bare the fundamental rights to free expression at stake in the Supreme Court hearing just days later,” a spokesperson said.
